title: Tyndale's last prayer (1536)
hook: strangled and burned, he prays: Lord, open the king of England's eyes

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Knox, the firebrand who planned schools for Scotland. Your line was a school in every parish.

A dinner argument in an English manor house. A young scholar named William Tyndale is debating a learned man, who says something that makes Tyndale lose patience. According to John Foxe, who told the story in his book of martyrs, Tyndale shot back that if God spared his life, he would make a boy who drives the plow know more of the scripture than he did. Erasmus had wished for a farmer singing scripture at the plow. Tyndale spent the rest of his life making that wish real, and it cost him that life.

Tyndale wanted an English Bible translated straight from the Greek and Hebrew, in words a farmhand could follow. In England he couldn't get permission, so he left and worked abroad, moving from city to city. His English New Testament was printed on the continent and smuggled into England, hidden among goods. Church authorities there bought up copies and burned them. Tyndale kept translating, and kept revising. Then a man who had befriended him betrayed him. He was arrested, held in a prison castle near Brussels, tried as a heretic and condemned. Foxe tells how it ended: Tyndale was tied to the stake, strangled, and his body burned. Before he died, Foxe says, he cried out with a loud voice: Lord, open the king of England's eyes. That prayer isn't a curse, and it isn't revenge. The king whose bishops had burned his books is the one he prays for, and what he asks for is sight. It echoes the first letter to Timothy, written in Paul's name, which says in the King James Bible that prayers should be made "For kings, and for all that are in authority." Some readers see an answer in what came after: English Bibles allowed in English churches, by the king's own permission, with Tyndale's wording carried into them. Some hear his phrasing in later English Bibles too, the King James among them. The last thing he's remembered saying asks for a leader to see clearly.

Picture someone with power over your life or your world, a president, a mayor, a boss, maybe someone you strongly disagree with, and let whatever comes up pass. Then, instead of an accusation, ask for sight: that they might see clearly. If you pray, borrow Tyndale's words, Lord, open their eyes; if you don't, simply hold them in mind without wishing them harm.
Tyndale. The English translator who, dying at the stake, is remembered crying out: Lord, open the king of England's eyes.
Your line: open the king's eyes. A prayer for sight, not revenge. That's day eight hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Christians in different churches pray for those in authority, often in set prayers during services; Tyndale is remembered as a translator and martyr, and some churches mark his day in their calendars.

notes: Claims rule: the year is in the index title only; no date stated in the voice. Foxe's wording is 'Lord! open the King of England's eyes'; Foxe is public domain but not on the validator's list, so the words are given without quotation marks and cited as a paraphrase. Confirm.
The plow-boy saying is paraphrased from Foxe; confirm.

Details (printed abroad; smuggled hidden among goods; copies bought up and burned; betrayal by Henry Phillips, not named; imprisonment at Vilvoorde near Brussels; strangled then burned) are from Foxe and standard histories; confirm each.

'Before long, English Bibles were allowed in English churches, by the king's own permission, and much of Tyndale's wording was carried into them' and 'some of his phrasing still lives in later English Bibles, the King James among them' are history claims beyond the cited texts; confirm or soften. Tomorrow's lesson covers Henry's break, so the king is not named here.
howItsDone: Tyndale is commemorated in some church calendars (e.g., Anglican, Lutheran); 'Christians in many churches' is a general claim; confirm or soften.

Editor pass: removed 'whose agents had chased him' (the arrest is not tied to the king's agents in the cited text) and the time claim 'before long'; cut the stock 'Christians read his story in different ways' line.

Second editor pass: the plough image now names its echo of Erasmus (day 849) instead of repeating it unmarked; cut the unsourced 'much of' (a quantity claim) from the teach and trapdoor and softened the King James line to 'some hear'; practice no longer calls 'Lord, open their eyes' Tyndale's own words.

Audit pass: Foxe calls Tyndale's opponent 'a certain learned man', not a churchman; fixed. Fixed the garbled double sentence ('meant to make it happen... spent the rest of his life making it true') and 'plough' to American 'plow' in the narrator's words. 1 Timothy now introduced as 'written in Paul's name' (authorship is debated).
